summary: This Standards Track document specifies carrying NTP client-server and symmetric mode messages inside Precision Time Protocol messages. This lets NICs that can timestamp only PTP messages do hardware timestamping, and allows delay corrections in PTP transparent clocks.

eli5.summary: NTP letters are put in PTP envelopes, because the network cards only stamp the times on PTP envelopes.

questions: how does ntp use hardware timestamping
what is a ptp transparent clock
subtitle: How to wrap NTP messages inside PTP messages so timestamping hardware and transparent clocks can help NTP.

tldr.problem: Some network cards can hardware-timestamp only PTP packets, not NTP packets sent to UDP port 123, and switches can correct delay only for PTP traffic. NTP cannot benefit from either.
tldr.mechanism: NTP client, server and symmetric mode messages are carried in a new organization-specific PTP TLV inside a unicast PTP event message. A new NTP extension field reports the transparent-clock corrections for the request.
tldr.outcome: NTP clients and peers can use hardware timestamps and, with one-step E2E transparent clocks, reach the same or better accuracy as PTP clocks. NTP broadcast mode is not supported.

today: RFC 10030 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2026. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 10030 defines a new transport for the Network Time Protocol (NTP). It encapsulates NTP messages in messages of the Precision Time Protocol (PTP, IEEE 1588). It covers the NTP client-server and symmetric modes. The NTP broadcast mode is not supported.

It adds two things: a new type-length-value (TLV) for PTP that contains an NTP message, and a new NTP extension field that gives clients and peers the correction of their requests from transparent clocks.

Using PTP messages means following the protocol rules of IEEE 1588. NTP over PTP does not require other PTP clocks in the network and does not disrupt them if they are present. Hosts can use PTP for synchronization in one domain and for NTP transport in another domain at the same time.
sections.eli5: Imagine putting your note inside a special envelope that the post office stamps with the exact time. The note is the same, only the envelope is different.

sections.title: Why NTP Needs a PTP Transport
sections.content:
PTP was designed for highly accurate clock synchronization in local networks. It relies on hardware timestamping in all the devices involved, such as network interface controllers (NICs), switches and routers. NTP can use hardware timestamps when they are available, but two issues get in the way.

First, some NICs can timestamp only PTP packets. Their receive timestamps are available only at a limited rate, so a hardware filter captures a timestamp only for packets that need it. That filter can usually be set for PTP transports and sometimes for the PTP message type, but it typically cannot be set to timestamp NTP messages sent to UDP port 123.

Second, switches and routers lack NTP support. With PTP they act as boundary clocks or transparent clocks. A transparent clock measures the delay in forwarding a PTP packet and writes it to the correction field of the packet itself (one-step mode) or of a later packet (two-step mode). Transparent clocks are specific to the delay mechanism, end to end (E2E) or peer to peer (P2P).

The RFC argues that client-server NTP, even over PTP, is more secure, more resilient to failures, better suited to networks without full on-path PTP support, needs fewer messages and gives clients an estimate of the maximum error (root distance). The disadvantage is that the transmit timestamping rate grows with the number of clients.
sections.eli5: Some network cards only stamp the time on one kind of envelope. Without this trick, NTP letters would travel without a precise stamp.

sections.title: The NTP TLV in PTP Messages
sections.content:
The new TLV carries NTP messages in the NTP client (3), server (4) and symmetric modes (1 and 2). Other NTP modes are not specified. It MUST be placed in a unicast PTP event message, because an event message is what enables PTP-specific hardware timestamping and transparent-clock corrections. The message MUST conform to PTP version 2, PTP version 2.1, or a future version that allows the NTP TLV as an organization-specific TLV. Any PTP transport that supports unicast, and an IPv4 or IPv6 mapping, can be used.

The NTP TLV is an organization-specific TLV with these fields:

  • type: 0x8000 (ORGANIZATION_EXTENSION_DO_NOT_PROPAGATE) in PTP version 2.1, or 0x0003 (ORGANIZATION_EXTENSION) in PTP version 2.
  • lengthField: 8 plus the length of the NTP message.
  • organizationId: 00-00-5E, the OUI assigned to IANA by the IEEE Registration Authority.
  • organizationSubType: 0x1.
  • dataField: two zero octets for 32-bit alignment, then the NTP message, which would normally be the UDP payload.
sections.eli5: The NTP letter goes inside the PTP envelope after a small label that says who made the rules and what kind of letter it is.

sections.title: Responses, Domains and Ports
sections.content:
A server or peer answering a request received over the PTP transport MUST reply with the NTP TLV over the same PTP transport. To avoid traffic amplification it MUST NOT send the response if the PTP message holding it is longer than the PTP message holding the request. This affects Autokey (RFC 5906), where some responses are longer than requests. The request SHOULD be padded with the PTP PAD TLV (type 0x8008) to the maximum expected response length. A response used for synchronization SHOULD have the same length as the request, so that delay is not asymmetric in networks without full on-path PTP support.

With PTP version 2.1, servers, clients and peers MUST check that received PTP messages carry the expected domainNumber and sdoId. The domainNumber SHOULD be 123 by default and sdoId SHOULD be 0. Domain 123 is not commonly used by PTP profiles, and the number SHOULD be configurable. Everyone using NTP over PTP in a network must use the same values.

If UDP is used for PTP, the source and destination ports SHOULD be the PTP event port (319). A client using port randomization (RFC 9109) would not get hardware receive timestamps, because the hardware filter matches only the PTP event port.

Authenticator fields in NTP messages MUST be calculated only over the NTP message after the TLV header. Other PTP data is not protected. Timestamps in the NTP messages SHOULD NOT be adjusted for where the NTP data begins in the PTP message. The transmit timestamp SHOULD match the PTP timestamp point, and the receive timestamp SHOULD be moved from that point to the end of reception.
sections.eli5: The reply must not be bigger than the question, so nobody can use the service to flood someone else. Everyone also has to agree on the same channel number.

sections.title: The Network Correction Extension Field
sections.content:
One-step E2E transparent clocks change the correction field in the PTP header of event messages that contain NTP messages. To use these corrections, the client or peer needs the correction of both the request and the response. The response correction is in the PTP header of the response itself. The request correction comes from the server or other peer in a new NTP extension field, the Network Correction Extension Field, with type 0x010A.

The field holds a 64-bit Network Correction in the NTP timestamp format, which has a resolution of about a quarter of a nanosecond. The PTP header correction uses a different format (64-bit nanoseconds plus a 16-bit fraction). Padding is the minimum needed for a valid extension field; in NTPv4 it is 16 octets, giving a 28-octet extension field that conforms to RFC 7822.

The value is the sum of the PTP corrections from transparent clocks plus the time it takes to receive the packet, which is packet length including the frame check sequence divided by the link speed. Adding the receive duration avoids an asymmetric correction when the two ends have different link speeds, since it cancels the shift from the PTP receive timestamp (start of reception) to the NTP receive timestamp (end of reception).
sections.eli5: On the way, helpers write down how long they held your letter. The reply carries that note back so the receiver can subtract the waiting time.

sections.title: Applying the Correction
sections.content:
A server that supports the PTP transport and receives a request with the extension field SHOULD reply with the field carrying the correction of the client's request. It MUST ignore the correction value in the request. A client or peer configured to use the network correction SHOULD include the field in its requests; for a client the value SHOULD always be zero.

With both corrections, the measured NTP delay and offset are corrected:

  • delta_c = delta - (nc_rs + nc_rq - dur_rs - dur_rq) * (1 - freq_tc)
  • theta_c = theta + (nc_rs - nc_rq) / 2

Here delta and theta are the NTP peer delay and offset from RFC 5905, nc_rq and nc_rs are the network corrections of the request and response, dur_rq is the transmit duration of the request, dur_rs is the receive duration of the response, and freq_tc is the maximum assumed frequency error of transparent clocks.

The corrected values MUST NOT be accepted for synchronization if any of delta_c, nc_rs or nc_rq is negative. This limits the error caused by faulty transparent clocks and on-path attackers. The root delay MUST NOT be corrected, so that the root distance stays independent of network corrections. If dur_rq is unknown, it MAY be assumed equal to dur_rs. The text gives 100 parts per million (ppm) as an example for freq_tc.
sections.eli5: The receiver subtracts the time spent waiting in queues from its measurement. It refuses any answer that would make a waiting time less than nothing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The PTP transport prevents NTP clients from randomizing their source port as described in RFC 9109, because requests and responses must go to the PTP port to get a hardware receive timestamp and transparent-clock corrections.

Corrections from PTP transparent clocks cannot be authenticated. An on-path attacker can change the correction field, but clients accept only corrections smaller than the measured delay. The RFC says the impact is comparable to delaying unmodified NTP messages. Existing NTP security such as Network Time Security (RFC 8915) still works over the PTP transport.
sections.eli5: The helpers' notes cannot be locked, so a trickster could scribble on them. But the receiver ignores notes that claim more waiting than really happened.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA created the "IANA PTP TLV Subtypes" registry under the "IANA OUI Ethernet Numbers" registry group, for organizationSubType values of PTP TLVs that use 00-00-5E as the organizationId. Subtypes are integers from 0 to 0xFFFFFF. The range 0-0xFFFF is allocated by IETF Review, 0x10000-0x7FFFFF by Specification Required, and 0x800000-0xFFFFFE is for Experimental and Private Use. Subtype 0x1 is "Network Time Protocol Message", and 0x0 and 0xFFFFFF are reserved.

IANA also allocated NTP extension field type 0x010A, "Network Correction", in the "NTP Extension Field Types" registry defined by RFC 5905.
sections.eli5: Two new entries were written into the official lists, so nobody else uses the same numbers for something different.

fields.desc: Transparent-clock corrections plus receive duration, in the 64-bit NTP timestamp format.

items.title: More secure
items.text: Network Time Security still works over the PTP transport.

items.title: More resilient
items.text: Each client can use multiple servers and detect failed sources.

items.title: Fewer messages
items.text: NTP needs fewer messages for the same number of timestamps.

items.title: Error estimate
items.text: Clients get an estimate of the maximum clock error (root distance).
